title: Efficient RL Training for LLMs with Experience Replay
claim: A replay-buffer method reaches higher accuracy at equal compute and stays stable, while the on-policy baseline collapses late in training.
layout: single line plot, compute on x-axis, shaded IQR bands, legend lower right
description: A single line chart plots accuracy (pass@1, y-axis from 0.72 to 0.76) against compute (x-axis from 0 to 35000). Two curves are drawn with shaded bands showing the interquartile range over seeds. The blue curve is the replay-buffer method, labeled (W,T)=(6,2), N=84. The red curve is the no-buffer baseline. Both rise steeply at the start. Blue then keeps climbing to about 0.762, always above red. Red plateaus near 0.75 and then drops sharply after about 27000 compute, falling below 0.72 with a very wide red band. The blue band stays narrow by comparison. Light grid lines and a boxed legend sit in the lower right. The eye goes first to the diverging blue and red curves and the red collapse on the right.
caption: Experience Replay improves LLM RL Training. Accuracy on MATH as a function of compute spent when training Qwen2.5-7B on OpenR1-Math-220k for the no-buffer baseline (orange curve) and a buffer of size 84 with (W, T) = (5, 3). We report the median and IQR over 10 seeds. Compute is calibrated so that a single weight update
abstract: While Experience Replay - the practice of storing rollouts and reusing them multiple times during training - is a foundational technique in general RL, it remains largely unexplored in LLM post-training due to the prevailing belief that fresh, on-policy data is essential for high performance. In this work, we challenge this assumption. We present a systematic study of replay buffers for LLM post-training, formalizing the optimal design as a trade-off between staleness-induced variance, sample diversity and the high computational cost of generation. We show that strict on-policy sampling is suboptimal when generation is expensive. Empirically, we show that a well-designed replay buffer can drastically reduce inference compute without degrading - and in some cases even improving - final model performance, while preserving policy entropy.
